group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department late this morning after experiencing three days of fever, progressive productive cough with yellow-green sputum, and a sensation of heaviness in the mid-chest that became more pronounced when he took a deep breath. Earlier that day his wife, concerned by an oral temperature she measured at 38.6 °C and a pulse she counted at the wrist of “a little over a hundred,” convinced him to come to hospital before reporting to his office job at a local technology firm. He ambulated into triage unassisted, speaking in full sentences, and immediately asked if he would be able to return to work the next day. His medical history is notable for a left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke four years ago that left him with only mild fine-motor weakness of the right hand but no cognitive impairment, and for non-ischemic systolic cardiomyopathy diagnosed two years earlier after an episode of acute decompensation; the most recent outpatient echocardiogram four months ago recorded an ejection fraction of 35 %. He follows closely with a heart-failure clinic, adheres to carvedilol, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone, and low-dose furosemide, and has maintained baseline functional status of New York Heart Association class II, routinely walking his dog two blocks each morning without shortness of breath. He denies any chronic kidney problems, liver disorders, malignancies, dialysis, or prior residence in an extended-care facility. There have been no hospitalizations in the past year, and he has not received antibiotics since treatment for cellulitis eighteen months earlier. He quit smoking cigarettes after his stroke, drinks beer only on weekends, and denies recreational drug use. Immunization review shows he received the current season’s influenza vaccine but has not yet had a second pneumococcal dose recommended for his cardiac condition. Review of systems is negative for headache, confusion, visual changes, abdominal pain, dysuria, rash, or lower-extremity swelling beyond his stable trace edema. On examination before any antipyretic, antimicrobial, diuretic, bronchodilator, or intravenous fluid, he is seated upright on the stretcher, appears slightly flushed, and engages appropriately with staff; he correctly states the date, location, and reason for visit, follows three-step commands, and performs rapid alternating hand movements without difficulty. Triage vital signs documented an oral temperature of 38.6 °C, heart rate 106 beats per minute in regular rhythm, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute with unlabored respirations, automated blood pressure 140/82 mm Hg confirmed manually, and pulse oximetry 91 % on ambient air. Skin is warm and well perfused; jugular venous pressure is estimated at 8 cm H₂O while seated. Cardiac auscultation reveals a tachycardic but regular S1 and S2 with a soft third heart sound similar to prior clinic notes, no new murmurs or rubs. Pulmonary examination discloses bronchial breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right lower posterior lung field with dullness to percussion in the same region, while the remainder of the fields transmit vesicular sounds without wheeze. No accessory muscle use is observed. Abdomen is soft, non-distended, with a palpable liver edge at the costal margin but nontender; bowel sounds are present. Extremities demonstrate dry skin, trace bilateral ankle pitting edema unchanged from baseline, and no digital clubbing. Neurologic survey shows intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength except for slightly reduced grip strength on the right, normal speech, and steady tandem gait tested briefly in the room. Point-of-care capillary glucose measured 136 mg/dL. An arterial blood gas drawn while he remained on room air registers pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 35 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 69 mm Hg. Initial laboratory panel obtained before any therapy returns hematocrit 31 % with hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 14.2 × 10⁹/L predominated by neutrophils, platelet count 210 × 10⁹/L, basic metabolic panel notable for sodium 143 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 103 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL—consistent with prior outpatient values. Lactate is 1.6 mmol/L. A portable posteroanterior chest radiograph obtained with the patient still breathing ambient air shows a dense consolidation occupying the posterior segment of the right lower lobe with air bronchograms; the cardiac silhouette appears mildly enlarged consistent with known cardiomyopathy, and diaphragmatic contours remain sharp. Electrocardiogram reveals sinus tachycardia at 104 bpm, QRS duration unchanged from prior, and no ischemic ST-T deviations. Two sets of blood cultures, a sputum Gram stain, respiratory viral panel, and urinary antigen tests for common atypical pathogens are sent prior to initiation of therapy; at the moment the emergency physician concluded the initial assessment, the patient had received no medications or intravenous fluids other than 5 mL heparinized saline to preserve arterial catheter patency, thereby preserving baseline physiologic measurements for subsequent risk stratification.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points using pretreatment findings.
1. Demographics: a man starts with his age in years, so age 47 = 47 points. No nursing-home residence = 0.
2. Comorbidities: systolic heart failure = 10; prior ischemic stroke (cerebrovascular disease) = 10. No malignancy, liver disease, or renal disease = 0 each.
3. Examination: alert (no altered mentation), RR 16 (<30/min), systolic BP 140 (≥90 mm Hg), temperature 38.6 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 106 (<125/min) = 0 each.
4. Tests: arterial pH 7.30 (<7.35) = 30. BUN 21 (<30 mg/dL), sodium 143 (≥130 mEq/L), glucose 136 (<250 mg/dL), and hematocrit 31% (≥30%) = 0 each. Room-air PaO₂ 69 mm Hg and saturation 91% do not meet the <60 mm Hg or <90% oxygenation cutoff = 0. Consolidation without pleural effusion = 0.
Total = 47 + 10 + 10 + 30 = 97.
Final answer: 97
